title:
Comment of Trevor Love in Docket(s)/Project(s) P-15424-000
Submission Date: 10/16/2026

documents.name: 151618.txt
documents.text:
Trevor Love, Lakewood, WA.
Re: DeepGreen Western Passage SPV LLC — Preliminary Permit Application, Project No. P-15424-000

I am writing as a private citizen in support of underwater data-center research, with conditions.

Large land-based data centers keep being sited in communities where their water use and power demand raise costs and strain infrastructure. Moving compute underwater, powered by tidal energy, is one of the few alternatives that actually sidesteps those problems instead of pushing them onto residents. I want to see this concept tested seriously — not blocked by default.

But "novel concept, novel problems" applies. The two legitimate concerns raised in this docket are noise and marine life, and they deserve real numbers, not promises:

1.  Make acoustic impact a permit condition. Underwater noise from tidal turbines, survey vessels, and construction will be the defining environmental question for this project. The permit's study phase should require publicly reported, independently measured acoustic-impact studies — noise budgets with actual decibel figures — before any license application moves forward. Sound dampening is an engineering problem with engineering answers; require the answers on paper first.

2.  Phase it small. The current application already describes a first phase of up to 16 turbine-generator units — the phased instinct is sound, and the permit should formalize it. FERC should expect measured acoustic and ecological data from a small initial deployment before any larger buildout is licensed. Small-scale proof is what makes the public willing to cooperate with the bigger version later.

3.  Independent review of the studies. Environmental studies paid for by the applicant should be reviewed by evaluators with no financial tie to the company, so the public can trust the numbers.

Endangered species protections must be respected in this process — North Atlantic right whales number fewer than 400 — but wildlife concern alone should not be a veto on innovation. The standard should be: measure the impact, engineer the mitigation, verify it independently, and scale only when the numbers hold.

A preliminary permit authorizes studies, not construction. The studies it authorizes are exactly what will define whether this project deserves a license — so the conditions should be set now.

Trevor Love
